options: High employee anxiety and burnout
A team where everyone knows the people around them are excellent
Constant turnover that disrupts cultural cohesion
Pressure to over-perform at the expense of work-life balance
quiz.explanation: Counterintuitively, Netflix employees report feeling more secure — not less — because they know their colleagues are excellent. In a mediocre team, you never know who's carrying whom. In a high-density team, you know everyone beside you is genuinely excellent. That clarity creates trust.

quiz.question: Google's research found that 360 feedback improved when:
options: It was tied directly to compensation decisions
Only managers provided input to keep the process efficient
Performance feedback was decoupled from compensation calibration
Feedback was delivered annually to allow time for reflection
quiz.explanation: When feedback is tied to pay decisions, everyone — givers and receivers — optimises for the financial outcome rather than honest development. Decoupling the two processes removes that distortion and dramatically improves the quality and actionability of what's shared.

lessons.title: Exit Strategy & Legacy
lessons.subtitle: Building a company worth acquiring — and a legacy worth leaving

cards.headline: Every Founder Exits Somehow
cards.body: Every founder eventually exits — through acquisition, IPO, management buyout, or simply handing the reins to a successor. The difference between a founder who builds something worth acquiring and one who doesn't isn't talent — it's intentionality. John Warrillow's Built to Sell and Collins' Good to Great both agree: the best time to plan your exit is 5-10 years before you want it. The company you're building today is either an asset that can exist without you — or a job that ends when you leave.

cards.headline: What Buyers Actually Buy
cards.body: Warrillow identified what acquirers pay premiums for: 1) Recurring revenue (predictable, low-churn cash flows), 2) Documented systems and processes (the business doesn't depend on undocumented tribal knowledge), 3) Management team (senior leaders who will stay post-acquisition), 4) Customer diversification (no single customer > 15-20% of revenue), 5) Strong brand in a defensible niche. Each of these is also what makes a great company to run — exit-readiness and operational excellence are the same thing.

cards.headline: The Succession Trap
cards.body: Collins found that level 5 leaders planned for succession deliberately and with extraordinary care. The trap most leaders fall into: selecting a successor who makes them feel secure (similar, dependent, non-threatening) rather than one who will make the company great. Great succession planning starts 5 years before it's needed, develops multiple internal candidates, involves the board, and specifically selects for the leadership qualities the NEXT phase of the company requires — not the phase you led through.

cards.headline: Legacy vs Impact
cards.body: There's a meaningful distinction between legacy (what people remember about you) and impact (what you actually changed in the world). The leaders in Collins' research who built the most enduring companies were almost uniformly uninterested in their own legacy — they were obsessed with the company's impact. Paradoxically, that obsession with impact rather than legacy is exactly what creates lasting legacy. Darwin Smith is barely known outside business history — but Kimberly-Clark is still a dominant company 50 years after his tenure.

cards.headline: Write Your 5-Year Exit Readiness Plan
cards.body: Score your business today against Warrillow's five premium drivers (1-10 each): Recurring revenue, Documented systems, Management team, Customer diversification, Niche brand. Total out of 50. Then pick your lowest score and write 3 specific actions to improve it in the next 90 days. Exit-readiness isn't about selling — it's about building a business that has genuine, transferable value. And that's worth building regardless of whether you ever sell.

quiz.question: The best time to plan your business exit is:
options: When you receive your first acquisition offer
At the point of maximum business value
5-10 years before you want to exit
When you have at least 3 years of consecutive growth
quiz.explanation: Exit planning is strategy, not transaction management. The systems, teams, recurring revenue, and customer diversification that make a company worth acquiring all take years to build. Planning 5-10 years ahead means you're building exit-readiness into the business itself — which also makes it a better company to run.

quiz.question: According to Warrillow, which factor most increases acquisition premium?
options: High year-over-year revenue growth
Strong personal brand of the founder
Recurring revenue with low churn
A large and growing team
quiz.explanation: Recurring revenue is the most valued acquisition attribute because it provides predictable, low-risk cash flows that a buyer can bank on. High growth is exciting but risky; recurring revenue is bankable. A business with $2M recurring revenue is often worth more than one with $5M one-off revenue.

quiz.question: Collins' research found that Level 5 leaders approached succession planning by:
options: Selecting successors who shared their personal vision for the company
Choosing successors who would maintain the status quo
Deliberately developing multiple internal candidates 5+ years in advance
Primarily looking externally for fresh leadership perspectives
quiz.explanation: Level 5 leaders were obsessed with the company's future beyond their own tenure. They started succession planning years early, developed multiple candidates internally, and selected for the leadership qualities the NEXT phase required — not the phase they personally excelled in.

lessons.title: The Leader's Lasting Impact
lessons.subtitle: Integrating everything you've learned into a leadership practice that compounds

cards.headline: The Compounding Leader
cards.body: Warren Buffett's most famous insight about investing is equally true about leadership: "The most powerful force in the universe is compound interest." Every one-on-one you run with radical candor compounds team trust. Every critical decision you make with the new management team test compounds your strategic clarity. Every time you look in the mirror instead of out the window, you compound your team's loyalty. Great leaders don't have breakthrough moments — they have compound habits. And over time, compound habits create extraordinary outcomes.

cards.headline: Integrating the Full Framework
cards.body: This course has covered three dimensions of world-class leadership: 1) Lead with clarity and courage (Horowitz, Grove, Scott, Lencioni) — the daily human work of leadership, 2) Scale the organisation (Harnish, Collins) — the systems and culture that outlast any individual, 3) Build lasting value (Collins & Porras, Doerr, Hastings, Warrillow) — the enduring foundation that survives disruption. No dimension works without the others. Clarity without systems creates a heroic bottleneck. Systems without clarity create bureaucracy. Value without culture erodes.

cards.headline: The Leadership Operating Rhythm
cards.body: High-impact leaders operate from a clear personal rhythm: Daily (one-on-ones, deep work, daily huddle), Weekly (team meeting, strategic review, one high-leverage decision), Monthly (culture reinforcement, talent assessment, stakeholder alignment), Quarterly (OKR review, planning offsite, succession conversation), Annually (BHAG review, culture reset, personal leadership audit). The rhythm isn't a calendar — it's a commitment to showing up with intention at every level of the organisation.

cards.headline: The Leader You Are Becoming
cards.body: The gap between a Level 4 leader and a Level 5 leader isn't intelligence, strategy, or work ethic. It's a small set of deeply ingrained habits practiced with extraordinary consistency over a long time: professional will (obsessive focus on the company's success), personal humility (window and mirror), radical candor (caring enough to say the hard thing), and a long-term orientation (building something that will outlast you). None of these are rare skills. They are all choices, made repeatedly.

cards.headline: Your Leadership Commitment
cards.body: Write three things: 1) The one leadership habit from this course you will practice daily for the next 90 days (be specific — "run weekly one-on-ones using the Radical Candor SBI model"), 2) The one structural change you will make to your business in the next quarter to move from good to great, 3) The legacy statement — one sentence describing the leader you are committed to becoming. Share these with someone who will hold you to them. The best leaders don't just know what to do — they have the discipline and the accountability to keep doing it.

quiz.question: The "compounding leader" concept suggests that leadership impact primarily comes from:
options: A series of bold strategic decisions at key inflection points
Hiring exceptional talent who multiply the leader's vision
Small consistent habits practiced over a long time
Developing a unique personal leadership style
quiz.explanation: Like compound interest, small consistent leadership habits produce extraordinary outcomes over time. A daily one-on-one practice, a weekly candour habit, a consistent mirror-not-window response to outcomes — these don't look impressive week to week. Over years, they define legendary teams and companies.

quiz.question: Systems without clarity in leadership tend to produce:
options: Scalable growth
Bureaucracy
Creative dysfunction
Over-reliance on the founder
quiz.explanation: Systems provide structure; clarity provides direction. Systems alone — without a clear why, clear values, and clear priorities — become bureaucratic machinery that processes inputs without producing meaningful outputs. Great leadership requires both the human clarity work AND the structural systems work.

quiz.question: The difference between a Level 4 and Level 5 leader is primarily:
options: Intelligence and strategic capability
Technical expertise in the company's domain
A small set of deeply ingrained habits practiced with extraordinary consistency
Access to better mentors and professional networks
quiz.explanation: Collins found that Level 5 leaders weren't smarter or more technically gifted. What separated them was a set of deeply practiced habits — professional will, personal humility, candour, and long-term orientation — applied with remarkable consistency over time. These are choices, not traits. They can be developed.
